MHHS2402 · Week 8 · Cardiovascular Regulation

Cardiovascular Regulation keeping perfusion optimal

Blood pressure can't be turned up with a knob — the body can only move four levers: stroke volume, heart rate, resistance and blood volume. This guide decodes how venous return, the autonomic reflexes and the kidney pull those levers, second by second and day by day, using the lecture's own figures.

Covers Slides 1–84 (all 6 learning objectives) Figures 21 plates from the deck Self-tests interactive

§0Framing · what can actually be controlled

What the body can actually control

There is no pressure knob — regulation works through four effectors and nothing else.

Cardiovascular regulation is defined as a mechanism that alters blood flow (and pressure) to maintain optimal perfusion. Like any control system it needs two things: an input — a measurement of some sensed variable — and an output — an action that changes it. The single most important idea of the whole week is deceptively simple: blood pressure cannot be controlled directly. There is no receptor the brain can pull to "set" pressure. Pressure is a product of other quantities, so the body must change one of those quantities and let pressure follow.

🤔 Predict · before you read on

If the brain cannot act on "blood pressure" itself, what are the only handles it can grab to raise or lower it?

Exactly four: stroke volume (SV), heart rate (HR), total peripheral resistance (TPR) and blood volume. Every reflex, hormone and drug in this lecture ends by nudging one or more of these — nothing else exists to pull.

Because MAP = CO × TPR and cardiac output CO = HR × SV, the full identity is MAP = SV × HR × TPR, with the added rule that mean arterial pressure is proportional to blood volume (MAP ∝ blood volume). To change arterial pressure at all, a regulatory pathway must change one or more of stroke volume, heart rate, total peripheral resistance and/or blood volume. This is the skeleton on which every later section hangs — whenever a reflex fires, ask "which of the four did it move?"

Reading a blood pressure: estimating MAP

Clinically we measure systolic (SBP) and diastolic (DBP) pressure, not mean pressure. But mean arterial pressure is not the simple average of the two, because the heart spends roughly two-thirds of each cardiac cycle in diastole. The weighted estimate is MAP = DBP + ⅓(SBP − DBP).

Reasoning · why weight diastole?

The arterial pressure trace is not a symmetric wave. Systole is a brief, sharp upstroke; diastole is a long, slow decay while the aortic valve is shut. Since the heart lingers in diastole for about ⅔ of the cycle, the time-averaged pressure sits closer to diastolic than to the midpoint. That is why MAP = DBP + ⅓(pulse pressure), not (SBP+DBP)/2 — the ⅓ is the fraction of the cycle spent in systole, and (SBP−DBP) is the pulse pressure it adds on top of the diastolic baseline.

Worked example · estimate MAP for BP 120/80

A healthy adult has a cuff reading of 120/80 mmHg. Estimate the mean arterial pressure.

  1. State the relationship. MAP is weighted toward diastole: MAP = DBP + ⅓(SBP − DBP).
  2. Find the pulse pressure (the term in brackets): SBP − DBP = 120 − 80 = 40 mmHg.
  3. Take one third of it: ⅓ × 40 = 13.3 mmHg.
  4. Add it back onto the diastolic baseline: 80 + 13.3 = 93.3 mmHg.

Answer: MAP ≈ 93 mmHg. (Note it lands nearer 80 than 100 — diastole dominates.)

Clinical / real-world

MAP — not systolic pressure — is what actually perfuses organs, so intensive-care and anaesthetic teams titrate drugs to a MAP target (commonly ≥65 mmHg). Because pressure can only be moved through the four effectors, every vasopressor and inotrope works on exactly those handles: noradrenaline raises TPR (and a little SV/HR), adrenaline and dobutamine raise HR and SV, and IV fluids raise blood volume. Knowing the identity MAP = SV × HR × TPR tells you which lever a failing patient needs.

R Recall — framing
  • Regulation needs — an input (a measurement) and an output (an action).
  • Blood pressure is controlled — indirectly — it has no knob; it is a product of other variables.
  • The four effectors — stroke volume, heart rate, total peripheral resistance, blood volume.
  • MAP identity — MAP = CO × TPR = SV × HR × TPR, and MAP ∝ blood volume.
  • Estimating MAP — DBP + ⅓(SBP − DBP), because the heart is in diastole ~⅔ of the cycle.
§1Learning objective · venous return mechanisms

Venous return mechanisms

You can't fill a pump you can't return blood to — five levers widen the pressure gradient back to the heart.

"Venous return" usually means blood coming back from the systemic circulation via the superior and inferior vena cavae to the right heart — but logically that same flow must also return to the left heart after crossing the pulmonary circulation, so a change in one becomes a change in the other. Return is governed by a simple pressure-over-resistance law: venous return = (venous pressure − right atrial pressure) / venous resistance. To increase return you either widen the pressure gradient (raise venous pressure or lower right atrial pressure) or drop venous resistance. Five mechanisms do exactly that.

Label Key — the great veins entering the right heart
Superior vena cava
Drains venous blood from the head, neck and upper limbs into the right atrium. Why it matters: it is one of the two collecting trunks whose inflow pressure sets the top of the venous-return gradient.
Inferior vena cava
Drains the abdomen, pelvis and lower limbs into the right atrium. Why it matters: most of the body's volume returns here, and it is the vessel the respiratory and abdominal pumps squeeze to boost return.
Right atrium (arrows)
The receiving chamber; its pressure is the "P₂" the returning blood must beat. Why it matters: the lower right atrial pressure falls (e.g. on inspiration), the steeper the return gradient becomes.

As Plate 1.1 shows, both cavae empty into the right atrium, so anything that lowers right atrial pressure or raises pressure in the cavae accelerates filling. Work through the five mechanisms in turn.

1 · Respiratory (thoracic) pump

On inspiration, the diaphragm descends: intrathoracic pressure falls (so right atrial pressure falls too) while abdominal pressure rises (raising IVC pressure). Both changes widen the (venous pressure − right atrial pressure) gradient, so more blood flows to the right heart. On expiration, rising intrathoracic pressure raises pulmonary venous pressure and pushes that blood on to the left heart. Net effect: more breathing = more venous return.

2 · Skeletal muscle pump

Label Key — the muscle pump in two beats
Muscles relaxed, valves closed (left panel)
At rest the vein is a passive, blood-filled column; the valves sit closed. Why it matters: this is the baseline — no muscle work means no active pumping, only the pressure gradient.
Muscles contracted, valve above muscle opens (right panel)
Contraction compresses the vein, spiking local pressure and driving blood through the now-open proximal valve (upward arrow). Why it matters: this converts each muscle movement into a stroke of a pump.
Venous valves
One-way flaps that snap shut when the muscle relaxes and pressure drops. Why it matters: they make the pump directional — without them, blood would simply slosh back down on relaxation and no net return would occur.

As Plate 1.2 shows, the muscle pump is a mechanism of dynamic exercise (rhythmic contraction–relaxation), not sustained isometric holding. During contraction and shortening the veins are compressed, raising local pressure and flow; when the muscle relaxes and pressure drops, the one-way valves in the veins prevent retrograde flow, so each stride ratchets blood one step closer to the heart.

Memory hook · the "milking" leg

Walking milks the veins upward; the valves are the one-way ratchet that stops the milk running back.

3 · Abdominal compression reflex

The CNS can command skeletal-muscle contraction — especially abdominal muscle — which compresses the large venous reservoirs of the abdomen, raising effective blood volume and venous return. The evidence is elegantly clinical: people whose skeletal muscle is largely inactive (for example, those who are paralysed) suffer far more frequent hypotensive episodes, because they have lost this reflex compression of the venous reservoir.

4 · Sympathetic venoconstriction

Label Key — where the blood actually sits
Systemic veins — 64%
The dominant reservoir of blood volume. Why it matters: constricting this compartment shifts a huge reserve toward the arterial side — the single biggest reason veins, not arteries, are the body's capacitance vessels.
Systemic arteries + arterioles — ~15% (7% + 8%)
The high-pressure delivery side holds relatively little volume. Why it matters: because arterial pressure ∝ arterial volume, even a small transfer into this compartment noticeably raises pressure.
Heart (diastole) — 7%, systemic capillaries — 5%, pulmonary vasculature — 9%
The remaining compartments. Why it matters: together they underline how little blood is anywhere but the veins at any instant.

As Plate 1.3 makes vivid, the venous system is a large reservoir of blood volume (~64% of the total). Sympathetic venoconstriction squeezes that reservoir: it shifts volume from the venous to the arterial side, which both increases the effective arterial blood volume (and thus pressure, since systemic arterial pressure ∝ systemic arterial volume) and increases return of blood to the heart. One action, two useful consequences.

Reasoning · why veins are the "capacitance vessels"

Veins are thin-walled and highly compliant — they can hold a lot of volume at low pressure, which is why 64% of the blood pools there at rest. That same compliance makes them the ideal adjustable reservoir: a modest sympathetic squeeze releases a large stored volume into circulation without needing to make new blood. Arteries, being stiff and holding little volume, cannot do this — they are built to distribute pressure, not to store volume.

5 · Gravity and hydrostatic pressure

Blood, like any fluid, responds to gravity — and low-pressure venous blood most of all. Because the venous system is so compliant, a change in body position redistributes blood whenever the hydrostatic column changes. On standing, hydrostatic pressure is far higher toward the feet than near the heart, so the compliant leg veins distend and pool blood in the lower extremities. This reduces venous return two ways: volume is trapped in the legs, and the blood that does return must overcome the taller fluid column. Standing is therefore a genuine challenge to filling — which sets up the orthostatic story in §4.

Clinical / real-world

These mechanisms explain everyday physiology and its failures. Soldiers who faint on parade are victims of lost muscle-pump action: standing rigidly still (isometric, not dynamic) lets leg veins pool blood, venous return and stroke volume fall, and cerebral perfusion drops. The fix is to flex the calves. Conversely, venous valve incompetence (varicose veins) breaks the ratchet in Plate 1.2, so blood refluxes and pools — chronic venous insufficiency. And patients with spinal cord injury lose the abdominal compression reflex, which is one reason they are prone to orthostatic hypotension.

R Recall — venous return
  • Venous return equation — (venous pressure − right atrial pressure) / venous resistance.
  • Respiratory pump — inspiration lowers right atrial pressure & raises IVC pressure, widening the gradient; more breathing = more return.
  • Skeletal muscle pump — dynamic contraction squeezes veins; one-way valves stop backflow on relaxation.
  • Abdominal compression reflex — CNS-driven abdominal contraction squeezes venous reservoirs; the paralysed faint more.
  • Sympathetic venoconstriction — veins hold ~64% of blood; constricting shifts volume to the arterial side (pressure ∝ arterial volume).
  • Gravity / standing — raises hydrostatic pressure toward the feet; compliant leg veins pool blood, cutting return.
§2Learning objective · impact on cardiac output

From venous return to cardiac output

Frank–Starling turns more filling into more output — and three atrial reflexes balance the books.

Venous return doesn't just fill the heart — it tunes how hard the heart beats. The link is the Frank–Starling law: an increase in venous return raises the volume of blood in the ventricle at the end of diastole (end-diastolic volume, EDV), which stretches the muscle fibres, increases the force of contraction (contractility), and therefore raises stroke volume and cardiac output. More blood in means a stronger beat out. But the same rise in filling also triggers reflexes that push the other way — so the section is really about balancing positive and negative feedback.

Label Key — reading the Starling curve
x-axis · end-diastolic volume (ml)
Reflects cardiac muscle fibre length — how much the ventricle was stretched by filling. Why it matters: it is the input (preload) that the curve converts into output.
y-axis · stroke volume (ml)
Reflects muscle tension / force of contraction — the blood ejected per beat. Why it matters: it is what the reflex is ultimately trying to control.
Steep lower portion (red arrows)
At low EDV a small change in filling produces a large change in stroke volume. Why it matters: the resting heart operates here, so tiny changes in venous return move output a lot — the reflex is highly responsive.
"Optimal length" plateau
The point of maximal overlap of actin and myosin, giving peak stroke volume. Why it matters: beyond it, extra filling adds little — the heart cannot keep trading volume for force forever.
Dashed descending limb
Where over-stretch would reduce force. Why it matters: the label states plainly it does not exist in the healthy human heart — the human ventricle is too stiff to be over-filled to failure, unlike isolated muscle.

As Plate 2.1 shows, the curve is steepest at low diastolic volumes: a small change in EDV there produces a much larger change in stroke volume than the same change would at high EDV. This raises the deck's own puzzle — how can the increase in stroke volume exceed the increase in end-diastolic volume?

Reasoning · how SV can outrun EDV

The trick is contractility. Cardiac contractility is the strength of contraction of the myocardial fibres; the greater the contraction, the lower the end-systolic volume (ESV) left behind. Since SV = EDV − ESV, stretching the fibres does two things at once: it raises EDV and — by increasing contractility — it lowers ESV. Both moves widen the gap between them, so on the steep part of the curve stroke volume climbs faster than end-diastolic volume alone would predict. More stretch doesn't just give the heart more to eject; it makes the heart eject a greater fraction of it.

The three atrial reflexes

Stretching the atria (the low-pressure, filling side) triggers three reflexes. Two of them reinforce the Starling response; one opposes it.

  • Bainbridge reflex (positive) — a rise in venous pressure is transmitted to the right atrium, distending it and activating venoatrial stretch receptors. These signal along the vagus nerve to the CNS, which feeds back to the heart via both autonomic arms, causing a 40–60% rise in heart rate. An additional ~15% comes from direct stretch of the sinus node speeding the pacemaker. Contractility rises too. The point: the heart senses it is being loaded and speeds up to clear the load.
  • Atrial (volume) reflex (negative) — atrial stretch is also sensed by low-pressure stretch receptors (sometimes called baroreceptors) in the atrial endocardium. This does two things: (1) releases atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), driving natriuresis (salt loss); and (2) signals the hypothalamus to reduce antidiuretic hormone (ADH / vasopressin), so the kidney reabsorbs less water. Both routes lose fluid via the kidney, lowering blood volume and therefore blood pressure — a brake on the very filling that triggered it.
  • Cardiopulmonary baroreceptors — the atrial/pulmonary-artery low-pressure sensors that underlie the volume reflex, monitoring the filling side of the circulation (revisited in §7).
Reasoning · Bainbridge vs the baroreflex — same stimulus, opposite HR

Both the Bainbridge reflex and the arterial baroreflex (§4) respond to "pressure/stretch", yet they change heart rate in opposite directions. The resolution is where they sense. The Bainbridge reflex senses atrial (venous filling) stretch and raises HR to pump the incoming load onward. The arterial baroreflex senses arterial pressure and lowers HR when it rises. So a large IV fluid bolus, which raises both atrial and arterial pressure, sets the two reflexes in tension — and the net heart-rate change depends on which side is stretched more.

Putting it together: increased vs decreased return

The deck's summary slides balance the ledger. Increased venous return has three positive-feedback effects that raise arterial pressure — it increases stroke volume directly (more EDV), increases it further through the Frank–Starling mechanism (more contractility, less ESV), and raises heart rate and stroke volume through the Bainbridge reflex — set against one negative-feedback effect that lowers pressure: the atrial volume reflex cutting blood volume. Decreased venous return mirrors this exactly: less direct stroke volume, a weaker Starling response, less Bainbridge drive (all lowering pressure), balanced by a reduced atrial volume reflex that lets blood volume rise back.

Clinical / real-world

These reflexes explain how the body handles a fluid bolus — and where it fails. In heart failure, the ventricle sits far along a flattened, low-lying Starling curve, so extra filling buys almost no extra stroke volume; the patient simply congests (breathless, oedematous) because the reservoir behind the failing pump backs up. The ANP released by atrial stretch (the volume reflex) is now used clinically: its cardiac analogue BNP is a blood marker of heart failure, precisely because a stretched, overloaded heart secretes it. And the atrial volume reflex is why lying flat or elevating the legs — increasing central filling — can transiently reduce blood volume via natriuresis over the following hours.

R Recall — return to cardiac output
  • Frank–Starling law — ↑venous return → ↑EDV → ↑fibre stretch → ↑contraction → ↑SV and CO.
  • Starling curve shape — steepest at low EDV, plateaus at optimal length; no descending limb in the healthy human heart.
  • SV outruns EDV because — stretch also raises contractility, lowering ESV, and SV = EDV − ESV.
  • Bainbridge reflex — atrial stretch → vagal afferents → ↑HR by 40–60% (+~15% from direct SA-node stretch).
  • Atrial volume reflex — ↑ANP (natriuresis) and ↓ADH → less water reabsorption → ↓blood volume → ↓BP.
  • Net balance — ↑return gives positive feedback (SV, Starling, Bainbridge) checked by negative feedback (volume reflex).
§3Learning objective · autonomic innervation

Autonomic innervation, the vasomotor centre & the vasculature

The medulla is the control room; sympathetic and parasympathetic fibres are its wiring to heart and vessels.

All the effectors of §0–§2 are ultimately driven from the brain. The neurons that control breathing and the cardiovascular system are concentrated in the lower brain — the medulla and spinal cord. This section maps the control room (the vasomotor centre), traces its wiring to the heart and vessels, and shows how tiny changes in vessel radius produce enormous changes in pressure.

§3.1The vasomotor centre

Label Key — the vasomotor complex and its inputs
Vasomotor centre (medulla)
The integrating hub for cardiovascular outflow. Why it matters: it is where sensed inputs become autonomic actions — note it is not the motor cortex, despite the name.
Vasoconstrictor output
Sympathetic drive raising vessel tone (and heart drive). Why it matters: this is the tonically-active line that sets resting vascular tone.
Vasodilator output
The opposing arm that can release constriction. Why it matters: lets the centre lower tone as well as raise it.
Motor cortex
A higher centre that communicates with the vasomotor centre. Why it matters: it is one of the pathways recruited during exercise — the brain pre-empts effort by driving the circulation.
Cingulate / orbital / temporal cortex, reticular substance, mesencephalon
Higher and midbrain regions that feed the centre. Why it matters: they explain how emotion, thought and arousal alter blood pressure — the input can come from "above".

As Plate 3.1 shows, the deck is emphatic: the vasomotor centre is not the motor cortex that controls skeletal-muscle movement — although the motor cortex does talk to it, which is one of several pathways used in exercise. Anatomically the centre has three functional areas: a vasoconstrictor area (anterolateral upper medulla), a vasodilator area (anterolateral lower medulla), and a sensory area — the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) in the posterolateral medulla and lower pons, which receives peripheral signals via the vagus and glossopharyngeal nerves.

The outputs split by side: sympathetic fibres extend from the lateral vasomotor centre and reach both the heart and blood vessels; parasympathetic (vagal) fibres extend from the medial centre and mainly reach the heart. Crucially, the centre only invokes a response when it receives an input — it does not act spontaneously.

Memory hook · lateral = wide reach

Sympathetic leaves Laterally and reaches Lots (heart and vessels); vagus leaves medially and mostly reaches the middle organ — the heart.

§3.2Innervation of the heart

Label Key — the wiring of the heart
Vagi (parasympathetic)
Carry vagal fibres to the heart, chiefly the atria and nodes. Why it matters: because they target atria far more than ventricles, they strongly slow rate but only weakly reduce contractility.
Sympathetic chain
Supplies sympathetic fibres broadly to nodes, atria and ventricles. Why it matters: the ventricular reach is why sympathetic drive can raise contractility so powerfully.
S-A node
The pacemaker; sets heart rate. Why it matters: its dual innervation is the physical basis of second-by-second rate control.
A-V node
Gates conduction from atria to ventricles. Why it matters: vagal slowing here lengthens AV delay — the mechanism behind reflex bradycardia.

As Plate 3.2 shows, both autonomic arms converge on the pacemaker (SA node) and conduction gate (AV node). Their power, from the deck, is asymmetric:

  • Sympathetic stimulation — raises HR from a resting 60–70 bpm to as high as 180 or even 250 bpm, and increases contractility by up to 200% (so stroke volume climbs).
  • Sympathetic inhibition — a smaller drop in HR plus reduced contractility can cut cardiac output by about 30%.
  • Strong vagal (parasympathetic) stimulation — can stop the heartbeat for a few seconds, reduce HR to 20–40 bpm, and cut contractility by 20–30%. This is smaller than the sympathetic effect on contractility because vagal innervation is mainly atrial and sparse in the ventricles.
Label Key — how autonomic tone moves the CO curve
Maximum sympathetic stimulation (top curve)
Peaks near 25 L/min. Why it matters: shows the ceiling — full sympathetic drive can nearly double normal output.
Normal sympathetic stimulation
The resting operating curve. Why it matters: the baseline against which changes are read.
Zero sympathetic stimulation
Withdrawing tone drops the curve. Why it matters: demonstrates that even resting sympathetic tone is propping output up.
Parasympathetic stimulation (lowest, dashed)
Vagal drive lowers output further. Why it matters: confirms the vagus can actively depress the heart, not just remove sympathetic support.
x-axis · right atrial pressure
Preload / filling. Why it matters: ties this back to §2 — at any filling, autonomic tone sets which curve you are on.

Plate 3.3 restates the identity CO = HR × SV graphically: autonomic tone doesn't change the shape of the filling relationship so much as lift or lower the entire curve, because it acts on both rate and contractility at once.

Worked example · sympathetic drive and CO = HR × SV

At rest a person has HR 70 bpm and SV 70 ml. Maximal sympathetic drive raises HR to 180 bpm and, by boosting contractility, raises SV to ~100 ml. Find resting and maximal cardiac output.

  1. State the relationship: CO = HR × SV.
  2. Resting: CO = 70 × 70 = 4900 ml/min ≈ 4.9 L/min.
  3. Maximal: CO = 180 × 100 = 18 000 ml/min = 18 L/min.
  4. Fold change: 18 / 4.9 ≈ 3.7× — most from HR, some from SV.

Answer: ~4.9 L/min at rest rising to ~18 L/min — sympathetic drive nearly quadruples output by lifting both terms of CO = HR × SV.

§3.3Sympathetic input to the vasculature

Label Key — where sympathetic tone acts
Arteries → arterioles
The resistance side; sympathetic fibres constrict small arteries and arterioles. Why it matters: arterioles set total peripheral resistance, so this is the main pressure lever.
Veins → venules
The capacitance side; sympathetic fibres constrict these too. Why it matters: this is the venoconstriction of §1 that shifts stored volume back to the arterial circulation.
Capillaries
Exchange vessels, shown without a nerve supply. Why it matters: capillaries are not directly innervated — flow through them is controlled upstream, at the arterioles/sphincters.
"Sympathetic vasoconstriction" fibres
The noradrenergic terminals fanning onto the vessels. Why it matters: they are the physical wiring for both TPR and venous-return control.

Beyond the heart, sympathetic (and parasympathetic) outflow innervates the resistance (muscular) arteries, changing their diameter and hence resistance. As Plate 3.4 shows, sympathetic vasoconstriction acts on the smooth muscle of small arteries, arterioles and veins, and in some tissues (e.g. mesentery) also on metarterioles and precapillary sphincters. The parasympathetic system does not innervate blood vessels — the exception being arterioles in the clitoris and penis, where parasympathetic stimulation releases the vasodilator nitric oxide.

Reasoning · why arterioles rule resistance (the 4th-power law)

Resistance to flow follows Poiseuille's law, R = 8μL / πr⁴, where μ is viscosity, L is length and r is radius. Because resistance depends on the fourth power of the radius, halving a vessel's radius multiplies its resistance sixteen-fold. The small, muscular, richly-innervated arterioles are perfectly placed to exploit this: a tiny sympathetic tweak of their diameter produces a huge change in TPR — and therefore in pressure — at almost no metabolic cost. Large elastic arteries, with far more radius and little smooth muscle, can't and don't do this.

§3.4The Windkessel model & MAP = CO × TPR

Label Key — the plumbing analogy
Pump = left ventricle
Drives flow (cardiac output) intermittently. Why it matters: it is the source of energy for the whole system.
Valve = aortic valve
Ensures one-way flow out of the pump. Why it matters: prevents backflow, so each beat adds to forward output.
Windkessel / air chamber = elastic arteries (capacitance)
Stores pressure during systole and releases it in diastole, smoothing pulsatile flow into steady flow. Why it matters: this "capacitance" is why blood keeps flowing to organs between beats.
Resistance nozzle = muscular (resistance) arteries, TPR
The narrow end that sets how easily flow escapes. Why it matters: tightening the nozzle (↑TPR) raises the pressure upstream — the arterioles of Plate 3.4.

Plate 3.5 lets us think of the whole systemic vasculature in a "lumped" way. Summing all the peripheral resistance gives the pressure inside the Windkessel (the large arteries). The mapping is exact: flow out of the pump = cardiac output, and pressure in the hose = mean arterial pressure. This delivers the master equation of the section: MAP = CO × TPR — tighten the nozzle (↑TPR) or push harder (↑CO) and MAP rises. Note the deck's caveat: the effect of sympathetic tone on the large elastic arteries is still not quantified, but because they are elastic and low in smooth muscle, they are thought to play little role in resistance regulation.

Worked example · MAP = CO × TPR

A person has cardiac output 5 L/min and mean arterial pressure 93 mmHg. If arteriolar constriction raises TPR by 20% with CO unchanged, what happens to MAP?

  1. Rearrange to find baseline resistance: TPR = MAP / CO = 93 / 5 = 18.6 (mmHg·min/L).
  2. Raise TPR by 20%: TPR_new = 18.6 × 1.20 = 22.3.
  3. Recompute MAP with CO held at 5 L/min: MAP = CO × TPR = 5 × 22.3 = 111.6 mmHg.
  4. Sanity check — with CO fixed, MAP scales directly with TPR: 93 × 1.20 = 111.6 mmHg. ✓

Answer: MAP rises from 93 to ~112 mmHg — a 20% arteriolar constriction alone raises pressure ~19 mmHg.

§3.5Transmitters, rate of response & the integrated picture

The chemical messengers matter. Vasoconstrictor nerve terminals release predominantly noradrenaline (norepinephrine), a potent vasoconstrictor acting on α-adrenergic receptors of vascular smooth muscle. Sympathetic nerves also terminate in the adrenal medullae, whose stimulation secretes both adrenaline and noradrenaline into the bloodstream, so these vasoconstrictors act systemically on most organs. Two nuances: adrenaline can cause vasodilation via β-adrenergic receptors on certain vessels, and it only weakly constricts skeletal-muscle vessels.

How is the CNS able to change blood pressure so fast — doubling arterial pressure in a few seconds, or halving it in 10–40 s? By acting on all levers at once: (1) constriction of most systemic arterioles (↑TPR); (2) constriction of the veins, boosting return and hence ejection via Frank–Starling; and (3) direct cardiac stimulation raising HR and contractility.

Label Key — the three arms of sympathetic drive
↑SA node firing rate → ↑heart rate
The chronotropic arm. Why it matters: raises the HR term of CO.
↑Atrial & ventricular contractility → ↑stroke volume
The inotropic arm. Why it matters: raises the SV term of CO by lowering ESV.
↑Vasoconstriction of veins → ↑venous return → ↑EDV → ↓ESV (Frank–Starling) → ↑SV
The venous arm. Why it matters: shows venoconstriction feeding straight into the Starling mechanism of §2.
↑Vasoconstriction in arterioles → ↑TPR
The arterial arm. Why it matters: the resistance lever of MAP = CO × TPR.
↑Cardiac output + ↑TPR → ↑arterial blood pressure
The convergence. Why it matters: every arm ends at pressure — the unifying output.

Plate 3.6 assembles §0–§3 into one figure: a single "↑sympathetic stimulation" signal fans out to heart rate, contractility, venous return and arteriolar resistance, and all four routes converge on ↑arterial blood pressure. The parasympathetic mirror is simpler (the deck's own overview): ↑parasympathetic stimulation → ↓SA node firing and ↓atrial contractility → ↓HR and ↓ventricular filling (↓preload) → ↓CO → ↓BP.

Label Key — parasympathetic vs sympathetic at a glance
Parasympathetic → heart → ↓HR → ↓CO → decreased BP
The single-route brake. Why it matters: parasympathetic control is essentially cardiac-only, so it acts mainly through HR.
Sympathetic → heart (↑HR & ↑contractility → ↑SV) → ↑CO → increased BP
The cardiac accelerator. Why it matters: two effects on the heart lift CO together.
Sympathetic → arterioles → ↑vasoconstriction → ↑TPR → increased BP
The resistance route. Why it matters: the pressure lever the parasympathetic system lacks.
Sympathetic → veins → ↑vasoconstriction → ↑venous return → ↑SV → ↑CO → increased BP
The capacitance route. Why it matters: the fourth pathway — sympathetic drive has three roads to ↑BP, parasympathetic has one to ↓BP.

As Plate 3.7 shows, the asymmetry is stark: sympathetic drive has three separate roads to raise pressure (heart, arterioles, veins), whereas parasympathetic drive has essentially one road to lower it (the heart). This is why the vasculature is largely a sympathetic story.

Clinical / real-world · vasovagal syncope

The lecture's own example: a large vagal cardioinhibitory response — triggered by emotional stress (bad news, sight of blood), physical stress, or blood-flow changes during urination, defecation, coughing or swallowing (the Valsalva effect) — slows the heart while a simultaneous vasodilatory response in the arteries drops peripheral resistance. Falling cardiac output and TPR together collapse blood pressure; cerebral perfusion drops and the person faints. The physiology is exactly Plate 3.7 run in reverse: instead of sympathetic drive on three arms raising BP, you get vagal drive plus sympathetic withdrawal crashing HR and TPR at once. Lying the fainter flat restores cerebral flow — gravity now helps rather than hinders venous return.

R Recall — innervation & vasculature
  • Vasomotor centre location — the medulla — NOT the motor cortex (though the motor cortex feeds into it during exercise).
  • VMC three areas — vasoconstrictor (upper), vasodilator (lower) and sensory (NTS, via vagus & glossopharyngeal).
  • Output split — sympathetic from the lateral VMC (heart + vessels); parasympathetic from the medial VMC (mainly heart).
  • Autonomic power on the heart — sympathetic HR up to 180–250 bpm & contractility +200%; strong vagus drops HR to 20–40 bpm.
  • Vessels innervated — small arteries, arterioles and veins (sympathetic); capillaries and most vessels are NOT parasympathetically innervated.
  • Why arterioles rule resistance — R = 8μL/πr⁴, so resistance varies with the 4th power of radius.
  • Windkessel mapping — heart = pump, aortic valve = valve, elastic arteries = capacitance, muscular arteries = resistance; MAP = CO × TPR.
  • Main transmitter — noradrenaline on α-receptors; adrenal medulla adds systemic adrenaline (β-mediated vasodilation possible).
§4Learning objective · baroreceptor reflex

The baroreceptor reflex — the short-term buffer

Stretch sensors in the great arteries damp every second-to-second pressure swing — but they don't set the long-term level.

With the effectors (§0–§3) wired up, we now meet the first sensor that drives them. Baroreceptors are stretch receptors located primarily in the carotid sinus and, to a lesser degree, the aortic arch. They provide negative feedback: the chain runs ↑pressure → ↑vessel stretch → signal to the vasomotor complex → ↓sympathetic drive and ↑parasympathetic drive. Everything the reflex does is aimed at pushing pressure back toward where it started.

Label Key — the sensors and their wiring
Carotid sinus
A dilated segment at the base of the internal carotid rich in stretch receptors. Why it matters: the primary arterial baroreceptor site — it samples pressure heading to the brain.
Carotid body
A small nodule beside the sinus — a chemoreceptor (not a baroreceptor). Why it matters: distinguish it from the sinus; it senses O₂/CO₂/H⁺ (§5), not stretch.
Hering's nerve → glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
Carries carotid-sinus baroreceptor afferents to the brainstem. Why it matters: this is the afferent limb from the carotid sensors to the NTS.
Aortic baroreceptors → vagus nerve (CN X)
The secondary site on the aortic arch, feeding the brainstem via the vagus. Why it matters: a second sampling point on the other great artery, giving redundancy.
Common / internal / external carotid arteries
The vessels that carry and branch the blood being sensed. Why it matters: orient the sinus at the internal-carotid origin — the clinically palpable spot.

As Plate 4.1 shows, the carotid-sinus receptors feed Hering's nerve, which joins the glossopharyngeal nerve, while the aortic receptors travel in the vagus — both reaching the sensory area (NTS) of the vasomotor complex from §3.1.

Label Key — the negative-feedback loop (to a pressure rise)
↑Arterial blood pressure
The disturbance being corrected. Why it matters: it is the sensed variable — the loop exists to oppose its change.
↑Stretch of carotid sinus & aortic arch → ↑afferent firing
The transduction step. Why it matters: more pressure literally means more nerve impulses per second (Plate 4.3).
Vasomotor centre processing → ↑parasympathetic, ↓sympathetic
The integration and output switch. Why it matters: a single input flips both autonomic arms in opposite directions.
↓HR, ↓contractility/↓SV, ↓CO + vasodilation (↓TPR)
The effector changes. Why it matters: lowering CO and TPR together attacks both terms of MAP = CO × TPR.
↓Arterial blood pressure (return)
The corrected output. Why it matters: closes the loop — pressure falls back toward normal.

As Plate 4.2 shows, when pressure rises: ↑stretch → ↑baroreceptor firing → the vasomotor centre increases parasympathetic and decreases sympathetic outflow → ↓HR, ↓contractility, ↓SV, ↓CO and vasodilation (↓TPR) → BP falls back toward normal. A pressure fall triggers the mirror image: ↓stretch → ↓firing → ↓parasympathetic, ↑sympathetic → ↑HR, ↑contractility, arteriolar constriction (↑TPR) → BP rises back up.

Label Key — firing rate vs pressure, in real time
Arterial pressure trace (top)
The pulsatile pressure wave in three states (normal, increased, decreased). Why it matters: shows the actual stimulus the receptor sees each heartbeat.
Afferent firing (bottom spikes)
Impulses in the carotid-sinus afferent. Why it matters: firing rises within each systole and overall with mean pressure — proof the code is instantaneous and rate-based.
"Increased" panel — dense firing
High pressure → many impulses. Why it matters: this heavy firing is what drives the strong parasympathetic/weak sympathetic correction.
"Decreased" panel — sparse firing
Low pressure → few impulses. Why it matters: the silence is the signal to switch on sympathetic drive — the basis of the orthostatic response.

Plate 4.3 makes the transduction concrete: baroreceptor firing tracks pressure beat-to-beat, rising with each systole and scaling with mean pressure. It is this rate code that the NTS reads.

Label Key — the sensitivity curve
y-axis · impulses per second
Afferent firing rate. Why it matters: the reflex's "input signal" strength.
x-axis · arterial blood pressure (mmHg)
The stimulus. Why it matters: lets us see where the receptor is most responsive.
Sigmoid shape
Flat at very low and very high pressures, steep in between. Why it matters: the reflex is nearly blind at extremes but exquisitely sensitive in the middle.
ΔI/ΔP = maximum
The steepest slope, near normal operating pressure (~80–120 mmHg). Why it matters: maximal gain where it is needed most — small deviations from normal cause the biggest corrective firing change.

Different pressures activate the baroreflex to different extents. As Plate 4.4 shows, the response curve is sigmoid, and its slope — the sensitivity ΔI/ΔP — is maximal near the normal operating pressure (~80–120 mmHg). That is a design feature: the reflex is tuned to be most responsive exactly around the pressure it is trying to defend.

Worked example · trace a baroreflex correction to a fall in MAP

A patient stands and MAP briefly drops from 93 to 78 mmHg. Trace the baroreflex response through firing, autonomic outflow and the four effectors.

  1. Sensor: lower pressure → less stretch of the carotid sinus/aortic baroreceptors → ↓ΔI/ΔP firing (fewer impulses/second, Plate 4.3).
  2. Integration: the vasomotor centre reads the drop in firing and flips its output → ↓parasympathetic, ↑sympathetic.
  3. Cardiac effectors: ↑HR and ↑contractility → ↓ESV → ↑SV, so CO = HR × SV ↑.
  4. Vascular effectors: arteriolar constriction ↑TPR; venoconstriction ↑venous return → ↑EDV (Frank–Starling reinforces SV).
  5. Result: in MAP = CO × TPR, both CO and TPR rise → MAP is restored toward 93 mmHg within a few heartbeats.

Answer: a fall in MAP unloads the baroreceptors, and the reflex raises HR, SV, CO and TPR together to buffer the drop — the physiology of not fainting when you stand.

§4.1Short-term buffer, not long-term controller

Label Key — the denervation experiment
"Normal" trace (top)
Arterial pressure over 24 min in an intact dog — a tight band around ~100 mmHg. Why it matters: shows the baroreflex quietly holding pressure steady beat-to-beat.
"Denervated" trace (bottom)
Same animal after cutting the baroreceptor nerves — huge swings from ~50 to ~180 mmHg. Why it matters: removing the buffer lets ordinary disturbances throw pressure around wildly.
Similar mean, very different variance
The average pressure is barely changed; only the variability explodes. Why it matters: the killer evidence that the baroreflex is a short-term stabiliser, not a set-point setter.

As Plate 4.5 shows (the classic Cowley dog study), baroreceptor denervation removes the buffer: the mean pressure is similar to normal, but the pressure now swings wildly. This proves the baroreflex is a short-term stabiliser, not a long-term controller of the pressure level.

Why not long-term? The receptors reset within 1–2 days to whatever pressure they are chronically exposed to. If pressure rises from 100 to 160 mmHg, firing is high at first, diminishes over minutes, then over 1–2 days returns to nearly normal despite the mean pressure staying at 160. So the classic view holds that they cannot set chronic pressure. But — the deck presents the counter-argument — experiments suggest they may not reset completely, and by influencing renal sympathetic nerve activity (promoting sodium and water excretion, lowering blood volume) they may contribute to long-term pressure control after all.

Reasoning · why "resetting" makes it a buffer

Think of the baroreflex as a thermostat that quietly recalibrates its target to whatever the room currently is. That makes it superb at damping fast disturbances (a cough, a change in posture) because it always pushes back toward "recent normal" — but useless at correcting a sustained shift, because after a day or two it simply adopts the new pressure as its baseline. Fast response, no long memory: exactly the profile of a buffer. Long-term pressure control is therefore handed to a system that doesn't reset — the kidney (§6).

Clinical / real-world · orthostatic hypotension & baroreflex failure

The orthostatic challenge (standing up) is the everyday test of this reflex: pressure dips, and a healthy baroreflex raises HR and TPR to restore MAP within a beat or two (the worked example above). When the reflex is impaired — in diabetic autonomic neuropathy, some antihypertensive drugs, or ageing — the correction fails and the patient feels light-headed or faints on standing (orthostatic hypotension). At the other extreme, baroreflex failure (e.g. after neck surgery or radiotherapy that damages the carotid sinus nerves) produces exactly Plate 4.5 in a human: labile pressure with violent surges and crashes, because the buffer is gone even though the average is roughly normal. A Valsalva manoeuvre can transiently trigger a faint by the same route.

R Recall — baroreceptor reflex
  • Baroreceptors are — stretch receptors, mainly in the carotid sinus (Hering's → glossopharyngeal) and aortic arch (vagus).
  • Feedback type — negative — ↑pressure raises firing, which lowers pressure back.
  • Response to ↑BP — ↑firing → ↑parasympathetic, ↓sympathetic → ↓HR, ↓SV, ↓CO and vasodilation (↓TPR).
  • Firing pattern — tracks pressure beat-to-beat, rising with each systole.
  • Response curve — sigmoid; ΔI/ΔP (sensitivity) is maximal near normal pressure (~80–120 mmHg).
  • Denervation shows — similar mean pressure but wild swings — the reflex is a short-term buffer, not a set-point.
  • Long-term — resets in 1–2 days, but may not fully reset and can influence renal sympathetic activity and chronic pressure.
§5Learning objective · chemoreceptor reflex

The chemoreceptor reflex

Sensors of blood gases don't just drive breathing — they also raise cardiac output and resistance.

A second class of sensor watches not pressure but blood chemistry. Chemoreceptors monitor the concentrations of oxygen, carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions. Peripheral ones sit in the carotid bodies and the aortic arch (the carotid body of Plate 4.1); central ones sit in the medulla. They detect three states, each with its proper term: hypoxia (lowered blood O₂), acidosis (raised H⁺, i.e. low pH) and hypercapnia (excess CO₂). Much of this was met in Week 3 for respiration — the new emphasis here is the cardiovascular arm.

Label Key — the two output arms of the chemoreflex
↑PaCO₂ → ↑CO₂ crossing the blood–brain barrier → ↑CSF H⁺ → central chemoreceptor firing
The central sensing route. Why it matters: shows CO₂ is sensed indirectly, as acid in the CSF.
↑Arterial H⁺, ↓PaO₂ → peripheral chemoreceptor firing (carotid & aortic bodies)
The peripheral sensing route. Why it matters: the carotid/aortic bodies are the fast responders to hypoxia and acidosis.
Respiratory centre → ↑RR, ↑TV → ↑minute ventilation → ↓alveolar PCO₂, ↑alveolar PO₂
The ventilatory arm. Why it matters: blows off CO₂ and takes up O₂ — the main correction.
Vasomotor centre → ↑sympathetic, ↓parasympathetic → ↑HR, ↑contractility → ↑CO, pulmonary perfusion
The cardiovascular arm. Why it matters: more output and perfusion move corrected blood faster — the CV contribution the deck highlights.
↓PaCO₂, ↑PaO₂, ↓H⁺ (↑pH) — negative feedback
The corrected blood gases. Why it matters: closes the loop, switching the stimulus off.

As Plate 5.1 shows, the sensed changes signal the CNS — both the respiratory and cardiovascular centres. Beyond driving ventilation, the reflex raises sympathetic and lowers parasympathetic output, which increases HR and contractility (↑CO) and causes vasoconstriction (↑TPR). Trace the central route in the plate: a rise in PaCO₂ crosses the blood–brain barrier and, via the bicarbonate reaction, raises H⁺ in the CSF — the acidosis that fires central chemoreceptors. Meanwhile raised arterial H⁺ and lowered PaO₂ fire the peripheral chemoreceptors directly.

Reasoning · why CO₂ is sensed as acid

Central chemoreceptors don't "smell" CO₂ — they detect H⁺. The link is the bicarbonate reaction: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. CO₂ is lipid-soluble and crosses the blood–brain barrier easily (H⁺ does not), so a rise in arterial CO₂ diffuses into the CSF, where the reaction runs forward and generates H⁺. It is that CSF acidosis the central receptors actually sense. This is why CO₂ is such a powerful, fast driver of ventilation — and why the corrective response (blowing off CO₂) runs the reaction backward and restores pH.

Clinical / real-world

The cardiovascular arm of this reflex is why severe hypoxia or asphyxia produces tachycardia, a surge in blood pressure and intense vasoconstriction — the body diverting a falling oxygen supply to the brain and heart. It also underlies the chemoreflex overactivity seen in obstructive sleep apnoea: repeated night-time hypoxaemia repeatedly fires the carotid bodies, driving sympathetic surges that, over years, contribute to sustained hypertension. And in the peri-arrest patient, the rising CO₂/H⁺ of poor perfusion is one of the last-ditch drivers keeping sympathetic output — and pressure — up.

R Recall — chemoreceptor reflex
  • Chemoreceptors monitor — blood O₂, CO₂ and H⁺.
  • Locations — peripheral in the carotid & aortic bodies; central in the medulla.
  • Three stimuli — hypoxia (↓O₂), acidosis (↑H⁺), hypercapnia (↑CO₂).
  • CO₂ fires central receptors by — crossing the blood–brain barrier and raising CSF H⁺ via the bicarbonate reaction.
  • Cardiovascular effect — ↑sympathetic/↓parasympathetic → ↑HR, ↑contractility (↑CO) and vasoconstriction (↑TPR).
  • Loop type — negative feedback — ↑ventilation and ↑perfusion restore blood gases.
§6Learning objective · blood volume & blood pressure

Blood volume, the kidney & the renin–angiotensin system

The slow lever — the kidney sets pressure over hours to days, and never resets.

The last effector from §0 is blood volume, and its controller is the kidney. The core rule is simple: systemic arterial blood pressure ∝ blood volume — raise total blood volume and pressure rises. But there is a catch that defines the whole section: this is not a rapid method. It takes a long time to change blood volume, unlike the neural reflexes (baro-, chemo-) or venous-return manoeuvres that act in seconds. Volume control is powerful but slow.

🤔 Predict · before you read on

The baroreflex acts in seconds but "gives up" after a day or two (§4). Which organ, acting over hours to days, takes over as the dominant long-term controller of blood pressure — and why can it succeed where the baroreflex can't?

The kidney. It controls blood volume (salt and water) and secretes renin, and — crucially — it does not reset the way baroreceptors do. Its ability to keep excreting or retaining fluid gives it effectively infinite gain over time, so it, not the nervous system, sets the chronic pressure level.

What the kidney does

The deck lists the kidney's many jobs — a reminder that pressure control is only one of them:

  • Ionic composition — regulates blood Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Cl⁻ and phosphate.
  • Blood volume — by regulating how much water is excreted as urine.
  • Blood pressure — through volume control and by secreting renin (the renin–angiotensin system).
  • Blood pH — by excreting H⁺ and conserving bicarbonate.
  • Red cell production — via the hormone erythropoietin.
  • Vitamin D synthesis, and waste filtration (excreted in urine).

The renin–angiotensin system (RAS)

The volume-and-pressure machinery works like this. Falling blood volume, or reduced renal blood flow (for example from sympathetic stimulation of renal vascular smooth muscle), induces the kidney to secrete renin into the blood. Renin, together with angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), produces angiotensin II — a powerful vasoconstrictor. That vasoconstriction increases resistance and therefore pressure (↑TPR → ↑MAP). Angiotensin II also stimulates aldosterone secretion, which drives Na⁺ and water reabsorption, increasing blood volume and again raising pressure.

Reasoning · why angiotensin II attacks pressure two ways

Angiotensin II is a belt-and-braces molecule: it raises pressure through both pathways of MAP = CO × TPR and MAP ∝ volume. Route one is fast and direct — it constricts arterioles, raising TPR immediately. Route two is slow and lasting — via aldosterone it makes the kidney retain salt and water, expanding blood volume over hours to days. Pairing an instant vasoconstrictor with a durable volume-builder is exactly what you want when perfusion is threatened: plug the leak now (TPR) and refill the tank for later (volume). It also explains why RAS-blocking drugs (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, aldosterone antagonists) are such effective antihypertensives — they cut both routes at once.

Clinical / real-world · hypertension & the RAS

Because the kidney is the long-term pressure controller, chronic hypertension is fundamentally a volume/RAS problem, which is why first-line treatment targets exactly this section: ACE inhibitors and ARBs block angiotensin II (cutting both vasoconstriction and aldosterone-driven volume), diuretics lower blood volume directly, and aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone) stop salt retention. Conversely, a narrowed renal artery (renal artery stenosis) fools the kidney into "seeing" low perfusion, so it over-secretes renin and drives secondary hypertension — a curable cause worth finding. And in heart failure, chronically low cardiac output keeps the RAS switched on, so the retained salt and water worsen the congestion — which is why RAS blockade improves survival there too.

R Recall — blood volume & the kidney
  • Core rule — arterial pressure ∝ blood volume — but changing volume is SLOW (hours–days).
  • Kidney pressure roles — controls blood volume (water excretion) and secretes renin.
  • Renin trigger — falling blood volume or reduced renal blood flow (e.g. renal sympathetic drive).
  • Angiotensin II — a powerful vasoconstrictor (↑TPR) made from renin + ACE.
  • Aldosterone — driven by angiotensin II → Na⁺ & water reabsorption → ↑blood volume → ↑BP.
  • Net role of kidney — the dominant LONG-TERM pressure controller, over hours to days.
§7Learning objective · cardiovascular responses

Bringing it all together — integration, time course & clinical challenges

Every pathway resolves to four effectors, staggered across seconds to days — and reads out in shock and haemorrhage.

The whole week collapses back to one identity: MAP = CO × TPR = SV × HR × TPR, with MAP ∝ blood volume. Every "determinant tree" resolves to the same four effectors — stroke volume, heart rate, total peripheral resistance, blood volume — fed by neural, humoral and local controls. This section zooms out to see how the mechanisms cooperate in time, why they oscillate, and how they play out in emergency.

Label Key — how everything feeds MAP
Mean arterial pressure (top)
= cardiac output × total peripheral resistance. Why it matters: the two-branch root every other factor plugs into.
Cardiac output branch → heart rate & stroke volume
HR from autonomic tone; SV from venous return, blood volume, respiratory & muscle pumps, cardiac-suction. Why it matters: collects all of §1–§3's cardiac story in one place.
TPR branch → arteriolar radius
Set by local metabolic control and extrinsic vasoconstrictor control (sympathetic + vasopressin/angiotensin II). Why it matters: the resistance side, tying in the RAS of §6.
TPR branch → blood viscosity
Rises with red cell number. Why it matters: a reminder that thicker blood raises resistance too — a determinant beyond the four effectors.
Blood volume → venous return
Governed by salt/water balance and fluid shifts, ultimately the RAAS. Why it matters: shows the slow renal lever feeding into stroke volume.

As Plate 7.1 shows, the tree fans out but always closes back onto CO and TPR: heart rate and stroke volume build cardiac output; arteriolar radius and viscosity build resistance; blood volume and the pumps feed venous return, and the RAAS/aldosterone feeds volume. There is nowhere for a control signal to go except through the four effectors.

Memory hook · the only four levers

"Stay Healthy, Track Volume" — SV, HR, TPR, Volume. If a reflex changes pressure, it changed one of these four — no exceptions.

§7.1The time course — who acts when

Label Key — the staggered defenders of pressure
Baroreceptors (peak in seconds)
Highest early gain, then fade. Why it matters: the fast buffer of §4 — first responder, but short-lived (it resets).
Chemoreceptors & CNS ischaemic response (seconds–minutes)
Kick in fast; the CNS ischaemic response is the powerful late-second surge when brain perfusion is critically low. Why it matters: emergency back-up when pressure is dangerously low.
Stress-relaxation, capillary fluid shift, RAAS/aldosterone (minutes–hours)
Intermediate-timescale mechanisms. Why it matters: bridge the gap between neural reflexes and renal control.
Renal–blood volume pressure control (days, gain → ∞)
Rises last but climbs toward infinite gain. Why it matters: the kidney (§6) wins the long game — it never stops correcting, so it sets chronic pressure.

Plate 7.2 is the unifying figure of the section: different mechanisms dominate at different times. Baroreceptors and the CNS ischaemic response own the first seconds; chemoreceptors and stress-relaxation the minutes; capillary fluid shift and RAAS/aldosterone the minutes-to-hours; and renal–body-fluid control the days, with a gain that rises toward infinity. This directly explains the §4-vs-§6 hand-off: the baroreflex is high-gain but transient, the kidney is slow but unrelenting.

Reasoning · why feedback loops oscillate (Mayer waves)

The baroreflex and chemoreflex are closed-loop systems — they change the very variable they sense. Any closed loop with a lag between detecting a change and delivering the correction will overshoot and undershoot, because the correction arrives late and pushes too far. The result is a slow rhythmic oscillation in pressure: Mayer waves, at roughly 0.1–0.15 Hz — one cycle every 6–10 seconds. Baroreflex-driven oscillations dominate at normal pressure; chemoreceptor-driven oscillations dominate at low pressures, where the baroreflex is weak (its curve, Plate 4.4, is flat at the bottom). The oscillation isn't a fault — it is the unavoidable signature of a delayed feedback controller.

Two threads run through all of this. First, the deck's insistent reminder: sympathetic and parasympathetic changes never "just happen" — each requires an input (a sensed change) to the CNS. Second, many receptors drive that outflow — the deck's non-exhaustive list of what signals the CNS: cardiopulmonary baroreceptors (atria/pulmonary artery, sensing pulmonary arterial pressure), arterial baroreceptors (aorta/carotid, sensing systemic arterial pressure), chemoreceptors (central + carotid/aortic, sensing O₂/CO₂/H⁺), pain receptors (skin/viscera), proprioceptors (movement), thermoreceptors (temperature) and higher brain centres (e.g. stress).

§7.2Cardiovascular regulation in emergency — shock & haemorrhage

Label Key — the four categories of shock
Hypovolaemic shock (↓CO)
Loss of blood volume (severe haemorrhage) or plasma-derived fluids (vomiting, diarrhoea, urinary losses). Why it matters: the tank is empty → less venous return → ↓CO. Attacks the volume/SV lever.
Cardiogenic shock (↓CO)
A weakened heart — the pump fails despite adequate filling. Why it matters: ↓CO from failed SV/contractility, not from lost volume — a different fix (support the pump).
Vasogenic / distributive shock (↓TPR)
Widespread vasodilation — septic (bacterial vasodilators) or anaphylactic (histamine). Why it matters: the nozzle is wide open → ↓TPR → ↓MAP, even with normal volume and pump.
Neurogenic shock (↓TPR)
Loss of sympathetic vascular tone (↓sympathetic nerve activity). Why it matters: the vessels lose their resting constriction → ↓TPR — the reflexes of §3–§4 have been cut off at source.

As Plate 7.3 shows, circulatory shock is simply a fall in MAP, and it is classified by which effector failed — a perfect test of §0's identity. Two categories crash cardiac output: hypovolaemic (lost volume) and cardiogenic (failed pump). Two crash total peripheral resistance: vasogenic/distributive (widespread vasodilation — septic, anaphylactic) and neurogenic (lost sympathetic tone). Naming the category tells you which lever to pull back.

Label Key — the whole toolkit responding to blood loss
Consequences (blue): ↓blood volume → ↓venous return → ↓SV → ↓CO → ↓arterial pressure
The primary insult cascading through §1–§2. Why it matters: shows haemorrhage attacking the volume lever first.
↓Firing of baroreceptors → cardiovascular centre
The §4 sensor detects the drop. Why it matters: the trigger that launches every neural compensation.
Sympathetic activation → ↑HR, ↑contractility, venoconstriction (↑venous return), arteriolar constriction (↑TPR)
The fast neural defence (§3). Why it matters: raises CO and TPR within seconds to prop up pressure.
↑Vasopressin & renin–angiotensin–aldosterone, ↑thirst
The §6 humoral/volume defence. Why it matters: vasoconstricts now and rebuilds volume over hours.
↓Capillary pressure → fluid reabsorption → ↑plasma volume; erythropoiesis → ↑red cells
The slow refill. Why it matters: pulls interstitial fluid into the vessels and remakes red cells — restoring volume and oxygen-carrying capacity over hours to weeks.

Plate 7.4 is the capstone: haemorrhage triggers a coordinated compensation that recruits every mechanism in this guide at once. The baroreflex (§4) drives sympathetic activation → tachycardia, increased contractility, venoconstriction (raising return via Frank–Starling, §2) and arteriolar constriction (↑TPR, §3). The RAAS and vasopressin (§6) add vasoconstriction and, with thirst, rebuild volume. Capillary fluid reabsorption pulls interstitial fluid into the plasma within minutes, and erythropoiesis remakes red cells over the longer term. All of it defends arterial pressure and refills the tank — the four effectors of §0, defended in concert.

Clinical / real-world · why a bleeding patient can look "stable" then crash

Plate 7.4 explains the treacherous course of haemorrhage. A young, healthy person can lose a substantial volume of blood and keep a near-normal blood pressure, because the sympathetic and RAAS compensations are maximally clamping HR and TPR to hold MAP up. Their pressure is normal but their reserve is gone — the tell is a rising heart rate and cool, constricted peripheries, not a falling pressure. Once losses exceed what compensation can cover, the props fail all at once and pressure collapses precipitously. This is why trauma teams treat the tachycardia and the mechanism, not the reassuring blood-pressure number — and why replacing volume (the failed lever) is the priority.

R Recall — integration & challenges
  • The master identity — MAP = CO × TPR = SV × HR × TPR, and MAP ∝ blood volume — everything reduces to four effectors.
  • Time course — baroreflex/CNS ischaemia (seconds) → chemoreceptors/stress-relaxation (minutes) → capillary shift/RAAS (min–hours) → renal control (days, gain→∞).
  • Mayer waves — closed-loop lag causes over/undershoot at ~0.1–0.15 Hz (every 6–10 s); chemoreflex dominates at low pressures.
  • Autonomic rule — sympathetic/parasympathetic changes never "just happen" — each needs a sensed input to the CNS.
  • Shock categories — hypovolaemic & cardiogenic (↓CO); vasogenic/distributive & neurogenic (↓TPR).
  • Haemorrhage response — baroreflex sympathetic drive, venoconstriction, RAAS/ADH, thirst, capillary reabsorption & erythropoiesis all defend pressure.
